A bus at a fixed interval

A resident counts as connected only if they can walk up to 500 m to a stop where an electric bus comes every 15 minutes, all day. Modelled candidate routes, not a confirmed plan.

Speeds are placeholders because no open minibus-taxi route file exists for Gauteng. Near-route figures count formal routes and mapped taxi ranks only, so they understate taxi coverage. Costs, ridership and day-to-day variability are placeholders. Roads have not been checked for width or condition, and the taxi industry has not been consulted.

Demand

What matters most

Each option is scored on four fixed scales: household gain from −10% to +10% of income, 0 to 5 net jobs per 1,000 residents, public subsidy from R40 a trip down to none, and taxi conflict risk. These weights combine them into a score out of 100.

Assumptions and sources
  • Household income: median monthly income for 37 metro sub-regions, from the Gauteng Household Travel Survey 2019/20 (CSIR, Table 9). Each zone takes the income at its rank on the Meta Relative Wealth Index, so it is an estimate for the area, not a measurement. The survey median was R4,543 a month and 30% of households did not report income.
  • Inflation to 2025 prices: Stats SA annual averages of 3.3% (2020), 4.5% and 6.0% (2021 and 2023), 6.9% (2022), 4.4% and 3.2% (2024 and 2025), a factor of 1.318.
  • Spending survey check: Stats SA's Income and Expenditure Survey 2022/23 puts median Gauteng household spending at R96,933 a year. That is well above what travel survey respondents reported, so the second income option scales incomes up to match it (factor 1.915).
  • Fares: Gauteng routes from Ivory Park and Midrand cost R18 to R35 after the May 2026 increase (The Citizen). The shortest listed trip, to Midrand, is R18, so a 2 to 6 km feeder is set at R14. The main leg is set at R26, the middle of the listed fares into Johannesburg and Pretoria.
  • Policy limit: nearly 60% of Gauteng households already spent more than the 10% policy maximum of income on public transport in 2019/20 (CSIR).
  • Value of time: the national minimum wage of R30.23 an hour from March 2026, valued at 50% for personal travel, following US DOT guidance. No South African standard was found.
  • Fare response: short-run elasticity of −0.3 for fare cuts, from Litman, Transit Price Elasticities and Cross-Elasticities (VTPI, 2025), which gives −0.2 to −0.5.
  • Taxi driver pay: a 2019 labour survey analysis found 70% of taxi drivers earned below the minimum wage (GroundUp). New feeder jobs assume R9,000 a month, above the full-time minimum wage of about R5,900.
  • Trip times: 5 minutes to reach a stop, then a wait of 5 minutes for tuk-tuks and 6-seat feeders, 8 for 16-seat minibuses (which fill before leaving) and 7.5 for the bus (half its interval). Vehicles average 15 km/h and people walk at 4.8 km/h, as in the Level 8 model. The travel survey found an average 14-minute walk to the first public transport in 2019/20.
  • Riders, fleets, vehicle prices, electricity and running costs come from the Level 8 workbook ('Vehicle options') and the 15-minute bus workbook. They are placeholders that need real quotes.
  • Taxi conflict: each zone starts from its Level 8 integration risk. Tuk-tuks lower it by half a level; 16-seat minibuses and buses raise it by one level because they compete head-on with minibus taxis. These adjustments are judgement, not data.
  • Jobs: crews per vehicle and taxi jobs per boarding follow the Level 8 workbook. Net jobs subtract taxi jobs serving the same trips; where taxi operators run the service, many of those drivers could move across.

Estimates for comparing options, not forecasts. Incomes, riders and costs are modelled, and no zone has been checked in the field or with the taxi industry.
